title: Too many edtech tools for teachers to learn: a Mac routine for 2026
metaTitle: Too many edtech tools for teachers to learn: a Mac routine
description: Too many edtech tools for teachers to learn? Check which apps run on your Mac, keep one job per tool, and learn one new app a week.

intro: Too many edtech tools for teachers to learn usually means your district licenses far more than you use. The fix is smaller than it sounds. Pick the few apps you use every week, learn those well, and set the rest aside. This page covers what the extra apps cost, why the list keeps growing, and fixes you can use on your Mac without buying anything.
tldr: Districts accessed an average of 1,417 tech products a month in the 2021 to 2022 school year, according to EdWeek.
The cost shows up as logins, thin training and hours each week. Survey figures vary, and many come from vendors.
Start with an inventory, keep one tool per job, and export your files before you delete anything.
Schoolwork is iPad only. Google Classroom is listed as web or mobile, and Canvas Teacher is designed for iPad.

blocks.text: Too many edtech tools for teachers to learn is mostly a licensing problem with a people cost. Districts sign up for apps faster than teachers can try them. Then you spend evenings working out which app holds which lesson, which login works, and which tool the team uses this term.
How many apps teachers really face

The best-known figures come from EdWeek. It reported that the average number of tech products districts accessed in a month rose from 548 in the 2017 to 2018 school year to 1,417 in the 2021 to 2022 school year. The article describes that as almost tripling. Those are district averages, not the count for one teacher.

Instructure's 2026 report gives a sharper contrast. It says districts have access to an average of 3,001 digital tools, while educators and students typically use about four learning applications. Instructure changed its method in 2026, so its numbers do not line up with the 2025 or 2022 reports. Treat the gap as a pattern, not a precise count.

Vendor surveys tell a similar story with smaller samples. A 2025 survey titled App Overload, run by Cornerstone Communications for Edsby, found 54% of respondents say their schools have 10 to 15 officially sanctioned educational apps. It drew on more than 100 teachers, 125 parents and 50 curriculum leaders. The study was vendor-sponsored, so read it as a signal, not a census.
What the extra apps cost you each week

Time is the cost you feel first. A 2023 Learning Counsel national survey asked schools how many hours a week teachers spend on digital tasks. Those tasks include finding materials, building lessons, and managing logins and assignments. The answers were 26% at 6 to 15 hours, 27% at 15 to 30 hours, and 24% at more than 30 hours. The sample size was not stated.

Pressure on time was already high before the apps arrived. The Learning Counsel article cites Pew Research's 2024 national teacher survey. It finds 84% of public teachers say they lack enough time during work hours for grading, planning, paperwork and email. Every new login competes with work that is already due.

blocks.title: Read the numbers carefully
blocks.text: Most app counts and time figures come from districts or vendors. Several sample sizes are not stated. Use these figures to spot a pattern, then check your own week.
The costs nobody puts on a budget

Money is the cost people expect to see, and it is the one I could not measure. I did not find usable figures for licensing spend. I also did not find reliable data that links the number of apps to grades or error rates. This page does not claim either link.

Privacy work is a cost too. EdWeek notes that varied tool choices make student data privacy harder to protect. Each app brings its own account, its own settings and its own data terms. Somebody at your school has to check each one, and that somebody is often a busy teacher.
Why teachers have too many apps to learn

Nobody picks a pile of apps for one job on purpose. Each one arrives with a reason. A principal buys a reading tool. A grade-level team adopts a math game. A platform adds a quiz feature that overlaps with both. Each decision makes sense alone, and the sum is a mess.

The operational side is the quiet driver. Instructure says the gap between access and use comes from the operational burden of managing licenses, integrations, privacy reviews and teacher training. You feel that burden as a password reset in the middle of first period.
Fixes you can use this week for free

Start with the list you already have, not the one you were promised. Most teachers can build a short, honest list in one sitting. The steps below need no purchase, no new account and no permission from a vendor.

items: Open Finder, then Go > Applications, or press ⇧⌘A. Write down every app you opened last week, including the ones you opened only to check a login.
Next to each app, write the single job it does for you. Keep the note short, a few words at most.
Circle every job that two or more apps share. Those circles are your overlaps.
Keep one app per job. Pick the one your students already log into, and the one that holds most of your files.
Before you drop an app, export your work from it. In Pages, use File > Export To > PDF. In Google Docs, use File > Download > PDF Document.

blocks.text: A short list is easier to defend. When a colleague asks why you dropped a tool, you can point to the job it did and the app that now does it. That answer carries more weight than a long debate about features.
Learn one app a week, not all of them

Feature tours waste time. Most teachers need only a handful of actions in a new app before it feels useful. Write those actions on a card. Learn them on the day you need them, not on a Saturday when you are tired.
Which edtech tools for teachers run on a Mac

Some apps your school names are not Mac apps at all. Apple's Schoolwork requirements page lists iPadOS as the only platform, with iPadOS 18.2 or later as the minimum. It does not list macOS. If your school runs Schoolwork, plan on an iPad for that part of your week.

blocks.text: Apple Classroom is the one Mac app in this group that manages a class. Its Mac guide says you can share webpages, EPUB books and PDFs with the class. Learn that sharing step first. It is the part most lessons need.
Check the data before you delete an app

Removing an app is not the same as removing its data. Student names, grades and uploaded files can stay in the account. Check your district's student data rules before you delete anything. Export your own materials first, then ask your district privacy contact what happens to the rest.

blocks.title: Student data comes first
blocks.text: Do not paste real student names, IDs or records into a new tool to test it. Use a sample file. Check your district rules before you use any AI tool with student information, Lazur included.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Ask where a menu is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to do something, and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click.

Lazur does not click for you. It does not edit your files or operate other apps. It is not a plugin or add-in for Pages, Google Docs or any other app, and it has no partnership with any app maker. You still press each button yourself.

The best use for Lazur here is learning the one app your school insists on. Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask how to add a footnote in Pages. The [step-by-step guide for footnotes in Pages](/how-to/add-a-footnote-in-pages) covers the same task if you prefer to read along.

Dictation helps with the writing you already do. Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. Add your own words to the personal dictionary, and save common replies as snippets. Parent emails get shorter when the phrases are already saved. See [reply to parent emails quickly on Mac](/for/teachers/problems/reply-parent-emails-quickly-teachers) for a routine.

For a tool you are evaluating, Lazur can run research in its own Chrome tabs through the Lazur for Chrome extension. It returns a summary and a report. Check each claim against the vendor's own page before you choose. A summary is a starting point, not a verdict.
Mistakes that make the list longer

items: Trying to learn every new app in the same week.
Starting free trials with real class rosters or student names.
Deleting an old account before exporting the work inside it.
Rebuilding the same unit in a new app because the new one looked nicer.
Adopting a tool a friend likes without checking the approved list.

blocks.text: A realistic next step for this week

Start tomorrow with the inventory. Keep the list in Notes or on paper, not in your head. Bring it to your tech coordinator, and ask which apps the district already covers. Then pick one tool to learn well and leave the rest alone until the term ends.

faq.question: Is there a number for how many apps teachers actually use?
faq.answer: Instructure's 2026 report says districts have access to an average of 3,001 digital tools, while educators typically use about four learning applications. Instructure changed its method, so compare it with older reports with care. Your own count from last week's logins matters more for your decisions.

faq.question: Can I ignore a new app my district rolls out?
faq.answer: Not always. Some tools are required by your school. Ask your administrator which apps are mandatory and which are optional. If a tool is optional, learn the one job you need from it and skip the rest.

faq.question: Do I need Schoolwork on my Mac?
faq.answer: Apple's Schoolwork requirements page lists iPadOS 18.2 or later and no macOS entry. Plan to use an iPad for Schoolwork, or ask your school which device it expects you to use.

faq.question: Does Google Classroom have a Mac app?
faq.answer: Google's help page says Classroom is available on the web or by mobile app. It does not mention a Mac app. Open Classroom in Safari or Chrome on your Mac, and check Google's help page again before you rely on any other claim.

faq.question: Is Canvas Teacher a good choice on a Mac?
faq.answer: The App Store listing for Canvas Teacher says it is designed for iPad and not verified for macOS. Use Canvas in your browser on your Mac, and check the listing for the current status before you plan around it.

faq.question: Does Lazur see my students' information?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored, according to Lazur's privacy notes. Your district's student data rules still apply, so keep student records off screen when you ask a question.

faq.question: Will Lazur learn the apps for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur points, explains, guides and dictates. It does not click buttons or operate other apps for you. You still press each button yourself, and Lazur waits while you do.

faq.question: How do I start if my budget is zero?
faq.answer: Use the inventory, the overlap test and the export step from this page. Those cost nothing. If you want voice guidance, a short Pro trial needs no credit card. Check the pricing page for current plans.

costs.title: Hours each week
costs.text: Teachers report real hours on digital work. A 2023 Learning Counsel survey found 26% spend 6 to 15 hours a week, 27% spend 15 to 30 hours and 24% spend more than 30 hours. The tasks include logins and finding materials. The sample size was not stated.

costs.title: Two to four hours on apps
costs.text: The 2025 Edsby survey, which was vendor-sponsored, found teachers spend an average of 2 to 4 hours a week using multiple educational apps. Much of that time goes to switching logins, menus and file uploads, not to the lesson itself.

costs.title: Time for work you already owe
costs.text: According to Pew Research's 2024 survey, as reported by The Learning Counsel, 84% of public teachers lack enough time during work hours for grading, planning, paperwork and email. Each new app adds one more place to check.

costs.title: Privacy reviews and student data
costs.text: EdWeek says varied tool choices make student data privacy harder to protect. Every extra app means another account, another set of terms and another place where student information can sit. Someone has to review each one.

costs.title: Money and results are not measured here
costs.text: I could not find usable figures for licensing spend, grades or error rates tied to app count. Ask your district for its total license cost before you assume the extra apps are free.

causes.title: Licenses get bought, not chosen by teachers
causes.text: Districts and schools buy licenses on their own schedules, often for a whole building or a whole subject. Instructure says managing licenses, integrations, privacy reviews and teacher training adds up across many products. A teacher often inherits a tool with no one to explain it.

causes.title: Several tools do the same job
causes.text: EdWeek says students interact with a range of digital platforms that often serve the same purpose. A reading tool, a quiz site and a slide add-on can all check the same skill. Each one brings its own login, its own settings and its own training.

causes.title: Training gets split too thin
causes.text: EdWeek notes it can be tough for district and school leaders to offer effective professional development. When many tools serve one purpose, each one gets a short session at best. The result is a shelf of partly learned apps.

causes.title: Pilots never end
causes.text: A pilot that finishes without a decision leaves the login active. A teacher tries a tool for one unit, then the account stays open with a class roster inside it. Ask who owns each pilot and when it ends, before it starts.

causes.title: Usage counts miss the fit
causes.text: The Learning Counsel article says usage counts can keep the most habitual tools while leaving instructional fragmentation unaddressed. Counting logins tells you which apps stay. It does not tell you which apps fit together in one lesson.

fixes.title: Inventory what you already open
fixes.text: Open Finder and press ⇧⌘A to reach Applications. Check the Dock, your browser bookmarks and the staff portal too. Write each app with the one job it does for you. This takes one sitting and costs nothing, and it gives you a real list to work from.

fixes.title: Keep one tool per job
fixes.text: Pick the tool that already holds most of your files. Keep the app your students already log into. Retire the others in order, starting with the ones you opened once or twice. A tool you open rarely is the first one to cut.

fixes.title: Export before you delete
fixes.text: In Pages, use File > Export To > PDF for each document you need to keep. In Google Docs, use File > Download and pick the format you need. Save the files in one folder named after the old tool. Delete the account only after the folder is complete.

fixes.title: Learn one app per week
fixes.text: Choose the app your class uses most this week. Learn only the handful of actions you will use on Monday. Skip the feature tour. Write each action on a card, and keep the card next to your keyboard until it feels normal.

fixes.title: Use the tools you already have
fixes.text: Pages, Keynote and Google Docs cover most lesson documents, slides and written feedback. Check what they already do before you sign up for a new app. A new tool has to be clearly better than the one you know well.

fixes.title: Keep one shared list
fixes.text: Ask your team to keep one shared document with each approved tool, the job it does and the person to ask. Google Docs works well for this. Link the document in your staff folder or your email signature so it is always one click away.

fixes.title: Ask one question before a pilot
fixes.text: When a colleague offers a new tool, ask what you will stop using when you start it. If nobody can answer, wait. A pilot without a stop date often becomes another login you forget about.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: List what you open
plan.text: Open Applications with ⇧⌘A from Finder. Write down every app you used last week, with the job each one does. Add the browser tools you use for class.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Mark the overlaps
plan.text: Circle every job that two apps share. Ask your tech coordinator which tools the district already covers. Write one line per decision so you can explain it later.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Export before you cut
plan.text: Export your files from any tool you plan to drop. In Pages, use File > Export To > PDF. In Google Docs, use File > Download. Save everything in one folder.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Learn one tool well
plan.text: Choose the app your class uses most. Ask Lazur to walk you through the three actions you need, or use the vendor's help page. Stop there for the day.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Share the short list
plan.text: Post the approved list and the job notes in one shared document. Name one person to ask questions. Pick next week's single app to learn.
